summary: Specifies a set of solutions for the replication and distributed operation problems raised when building an Internet Directory using X.500 (1988). It was on the standards track and is now historic.

eli5.summary: It gives answers for how to keep copies of a big directory in many places. It is now historic.

questions: what is an entry data block
what is spot shadowing in x.500
subtitle: An interim recipe for copying and sharing X.500 directory data across the Internet, since replaced by waiting for the standard.

tldr.problem: Building an Internet-wide directory on X.500(1988) needs replication and workable distributed operations over networks that are not all interconnected, and no stable standard solution existed yet.
tldr.mechanism: The memo documents the approach already used in the QUIPU implementation: replicate whole blocks of entries (Entry Data Blocks) with a simple pull operation, and add rules for relaying queries between separate network communities.
tldr.outcome: The authors said the procedures were an INTERIM approach with known manageability and scalability deficiencies, to be obsoleted once standards arrived. The RFC is now Historic.

today: RFC 1276 is Historic according to the unit metadata, and no replacement RFC is recorded for it. The text itself says it was an interim approach that would be obsoleted when standards were available. Its requirements are in RFC 1275.

sections.title: Why an Interim Approach
sections.content:
The authors say a number of requirements, described in RFC 1275, must be met before a directory can be deployed on the Internet, and the standards bodies had no stable solution yet. Trying to intercept the future standard would be awkward, the target keeps moving, and the delay would make it too late for a quick start.

Instead this memo documents what is already done in operation, which is simpler, cheaper to implement and quick to start. It repeats that this is an INTERIM approach with known deficiencies in manageability and scalability, and that it will be obsoleted once standard approaches are available.
sections.eli5: The official rules were not ready, so the authors write down the simple way that people already use, and say it is only for now.

sections.title: Distributed Operations Across Communities
sections.content:
X.500 assumes all its components can reach each other. On the Internet pilot, servers might use TCP/IP, TP4/CLNS or TP0/CONS. The memo defines a community as an environment where direct network communication is possible, identified by a set of network address prefixes. Two entities with a common community can talk directly.

Two extensions follow. First, a server that would rather answer with a referral may do so only if it believes the caller can connect directly to the referred-to server; otherwise it must chain the query itself. Second, a server following a referral it cannot reach directly either passes the query to the server it would use for the entry one level higher in the tree, or uses a manually configured relay DSA that belongs to both communities. Conforming servers follow these procedures; the memo places no requirements on user agents.

It also lets a referral name master and slave copies by giving a subordinate reference with multiple values, the first being the master.
sections.eli5: If you cannot reach a library directly, you ask a friend who can reach both of you to pass the question along.

sections.title: The Entry Data Block
sections.content:
The unit of replication is not a single entry but the complete set of immediate children of an entry, called an Entry Data Block (EDB). It is named by its parent and holds each child's relative distinguished name, attributes and knowledge information. A server that holds non-cached information on an entry holds all its siblings.

One server holds the master EDB, which contains entries it masters plus slave copies of entries mastered elsewhere, which it keeps up to date automatically. Other servers may hold slave EDBs copied from the master. The stated benefits are simpler and faster name resolution and good performance for single-level searching and listing, which could otherwise touch very many servers.
sections.eli5: Instead of copying one page at a time, you copy a whole chapter, so the copy is always complete for that part of the book.

sections.title: Naming Servers and Representing Knowledge
sections.content:
All servers must be named in the directory tree, with the master presentation address stored in that entry. To avoid deadlock in finding a server's address, a well-known server with root knowledge is used and servers are named high in the tree. Detailed naming policy was left to a future RFC.

Knowledge is kept in the tree using knowledge attributes, in four kinds of entry: a leaf mastered here; an entry whose level below has an EDB (using the new InternetDSNonLeafObject class with masterDSA and optional slaveDSA); an entry mastered in a server not following this memo, handled by spot shadowing, where the master EDB holder reads the entry with a standard DSP Read; and entries below held in servers that are indicated by non-specific subordinate references. A second class, ExternalDSObject, carries the standard references with an optional presentation address.
sections.eli5: Each page of the directory says where the master copy lives and where spare copies are kept, like a note saying which shelf has the original.

sections.title: The Replication Operation
sections.content:
Replication uses one remote operation, GetEntryDataBlock, which pulls an EDB. Normally the initiator sends the EDB version it holds (sendIfMoreRecentThan) and gets the whole EDB only if the responder's copy is newer. Options ask for just the version number or force full retrieval.

Moving a large EDB in one operation gives very large PDUs, so the initiator may set maxEntries and the responder returns nextEntryPosition to continue in chunks. The memo notes this is simple but less efficient than an incremental technique, which it expects a standard to supply. It lists three ways to handle updates during a multi-operation transfer (block updates, keep the old version until the transfer ends, or let the transfer fail), and the protocol should transfer only user attributes. A new application context called "Internet DSP" lets a server advertise support.
sections.eli5: You ask 'is your copy newer than mine?' and if it is, you receive the pages, in small batches if there are many.

sections.title: Scaling, Use and Security
sections.content:
The main scaling limit is the non-incremental update. With an average entry size of around a thousand bytes and a maximum reasonable transfer size of tens of megabytes, the fanout limit is of order 10 000, so the technique is meant only for high levels of the tree. It does not preclude other replication techniques.

Applications should allow normal reads to use copy data, but repeat the request with copies prohibited by service controls if they suspect stale information. The memo states that security considerations are not discussed.
sections.eli5: Copying everything each time only works for fairly small books, so this trick is meant for the top of the directory, not every detail.
